HAWAII MONITORING CATEGORY 5 HURRICANE LOWELL‼️🌀Lowell has regained Category 5 strength with sustained winds of 160 mph. The center is forecast to pass west of Hawaii late Monday into Monday night, potentially near major-hurricane strength. A direct landfall is not currently forecast, but storm surge and damaging-wind impacts remain possible, particularly across Kauai County. Watches will likely be issued Saturday.

Heavy rain should spread across the islands Sunday afternoon and continue into early next week. Forecast totals generally range from 2-8 inches, with isolated amounts near 10 inches possible along favored south-and southeast-facing slopes. Flash flooding and landslides will be possible, especially near steep terrain.

Lowell will also generate increasingly dangerous, potentially life-threatening surf and rip currents. Extra-large waves could affect southern and western shores early next week, while high tides increase the risk of coastal flooding and impacts to roads, properties, harbors and channel entrances.

Kauai and Niihau currently face the greatest risk, but impacts are possible across the entire island chain. Residents should review hurricane plans and closely monitor forecasts, as even a small track adjustment could substantially change the expected conditions. This is what radar could look like as the Hurricane passes just west of the Islands late Monday🌀

WHAT IS HAPPENING? Local radar sites around the Great Lakes and New England are exploding with radar returns this evening. It's not rain. 

These are "biological" echoes, many millions of birds participating in the annual fall migration southward. These large nocturnal migrations appear as fuzzy circles around individual radar sites, flaring up after dark as birds take flight under the relative safety of night. You'll often see them appear shortly after local sunset, expanding westward as the Earth rotates. Pretty cool!

HURRICANE MARIE MOISTURE SURGES INTO SW🌧️🌴⚠️Hurricane Marie will remain well offshore, but a plume of its tropical moisture will get pulled north and northeast across parts of the Southwest this Labor Day Weekend. Rain chances begin increasing Saturday, but Sunday looks like the main day for widespread showers, thunderstorms and locally heavy rain from Southern California northeast through the Mojave Desert, southern Nevada, northwestern Arizona and Utah.

Southern California will see increasing tropical moisture Saturday into Sunday. Around Los Angeles, Sunday currently has the greatest rain potential, with most locations expected to receive less than 0.50" and many under 0.25", although locally higher totals are possible in the mountains or beneath heavier showers. San Diego and surrounding areas have a lower overall rainfall signal, but scattered showers remain possible, especially Sunday.

Farther northeast, the moisture plume becomes more impressive. Across southern Nevada, southeastern California and northwestern Arizona, a band of rain is expected to develop Sunday. Current projections generally favor 0.250.50", but locally heavier amounts will be possible depending on exactly where the rain band sets up. Northern Arizona will also see increasing moisture, with Sunday bringing the greatest rain and thunderstorm coverage, especially across northwestern Arizona and near the Grand Canyon.

Utah may end up beneath one of the more favorable setups for heavier rainfall. Tropical moisture interacting with a strong upper-level disturbance should produce widespread, quick-moving showers and thunderstorms Sunday. The Weather Prediction Center has placed a corridor from near Las Vegas and the Grand Canyon northeastward through portions of Utah in the best chance to see excessive rainfall and some flooding, including areas around Zion and Bryce Canyon. Slot canyons, normally dry washes, burn scars and other flood-prone terrain could become particularly dangerous if heavier rain develops.

This does not mean everyone will see heavy rain or that it will rain throughout the entire holiday weekend. Saturday looks more scattered, while Sunday currently has the strongest signal for a broader surge of tropical moisture and locally heavy rainfall. Where heavier showers or thunderstorms develop, localized flash flooding will be possible, especially across the deserts, mountains and slot-canyon country🌧️🌴⚠️

MONITORING MARIE | 2 ROUNDS OF MOISTURE🌧️🌴Hurricane Marie is expected to remain well offshore of California, but its tropical moisture could influence parts of the West in multiple waves over the next week! The first push arrives this weekend as moisture from Marie is pulled northward ahead of a trough along the West Coast. Southern California should see increasing clouds and shower chances Saturday into Sunday, with Sunday looking like the wetter day. A few thunderstorms will also be possible, especially across the mountains and deserts. This deeper moisture will spread into southeast California and southern Nevada, into Utah and northern Arizona, bringing an increase in showers and thunderstorms there as well. Farther north across the Great Basin and interior Northwest, additional rain is expected into early next week, although not all of that moisture can necessarily be directly attributed to Marie.

Then attention turns to a possible second push of tropical moisture during the middle to latter part of next week. Forecast confidence is much lower with this round, but there continues to be a signal for another trough to develop over the Eastern Pacific while Marie weakens well offshore. That pattern could potentially draw additional remnant tropical moisture northward into California and portions of the West.

Importantly, this does not mean Marie is forecast to hit California. The circulation itself should remain well offshore and weaken. The story is the moisture being pulled away from the system and transported northward. Exactly how much moisture reaches the West - and where it goes - will depend heavily on the evolution of Marie and the Pacific trough, so the mid-to-late week portion of the forecast remains something to monitor🌧️🌴

ACTIVE PATTERN MAY CONTINUE FOR WEST🌧️🌲a persistent trough near the West Coast, combined with an active Eastern Pacific, is expected to favor more opportunities for moisture across a large portion of the West! Tropical moisture could occasionally become involved as well, potentially enhancing rainfall at times. The overall pattern favors above-normal precipitation across much of the West, particularly from the Pacific Northwest and Northern U.S. Rockies southward into parts of the Great Basin and Southwest.

It’s important to remember what a wetter-than-normal outlook actually means. This does not mean it will rain every day, nor does it mean every location will see significant rainfall. The takeaway is the overall signal: the pattern should be more favorable than normal for periodic rain and storm systems across the West, with multiple opportunities for moisture rather than one continuous stretch of wet weather. This wetter signal could persist for a while as troughing remains near the West Coast and Pacific moisture continues to feed into the region🌧️🌲

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text:
MORE THUNDERSTORMS ACROSS THE NORTHWEST TODAY⛈️a cold upper-level storm system remains over the Pacific Northwest, keeping temperatures unusually cool while creating enough instability for another round of showers and thunderstorms. Across western Washington, showers and isolated thunderstorms will redevelop, particularly near the Cascades, with some activity potentially drifting toward the lowlands. Western Oregon will see increasing thunderstorm chances late this morning and afternoon, especially south of Portland and around the Coast Range and Cascades. Some of the better thunderstorm coverage will extend across southern and central Oregon, including around Bend, before spreading into eastern Oregon and southwest Idaho. Scattered thunderstorms are also possible across eastern Washington, northern Idaho and portions of western Montana.

Severe weather is not the main concern, but stronger cells could produce brief heavy rain, small hail, frequent lightning and locally gusty winds. Storm movement may be slow in some areas, allowing localized heavier rainfall. Given the cold upper low, steep low-level lapse rates and weakly sheared-showery environment, a low-end cold-air funnel is possible, particularly across western Washington and Oregon. Most funnels in this type of environment are brief and remain harmless, although a very small percentage can occasionally reach the ground. Overall, the greatest thunderstorm coverage today should favor Oregon into southwest Idaho⛈️

items.text: Hurricane Hunters are specialized military and civilian aircrews who fly directly into tropical cyclones to gather critical, real-time weather data. Operating highly instrumented aircrafts, they deploy sensors like dropsondes into the eye of the storm to measure wind speed, air pressure, temperature, and humidity from the inside out. This extreme, hands-on data collection provides the precise information needed to build accurate forecasting models, predict a storm's path and intensity, and issue life-saving evacuation warnings.

items.author: ericsnitilwx
items.text:
ARE WE SEEING MORE TORNADOES? It's a reasonable question to ask. The state of New York is now up to 20 confirmed tornadoes this year. On average (based on 2006-2025 data), New York sees about 9 tornadoes per year. So, we've already doubled that figure in 2026. 

Also heavily biasing our recent memory is what took place in 2024 when we shattered records with 32 confirmed tornadoes. Looking at data dating back to the 1950s, there is most certainly a trendline toward increasing tornado counts in time (smoothing out the inherent variability for individual years) in New York.

The bigger question is, why? That's a more complex answer. The answer is certainly not limited to the idea that we're simply having more tornadoes forming in New York than we did in the past. Technology has improved dramatically. Boots on the ground with eyes on storms has increased dramatically. Video & photo evidence (everyone has a smartphone in their pocket) has increased dramatically. Put another way, our ability to DETECT & CONFIRM tornadoes plays a role in the increasing numbers. 

So, are we having more tornadoes? Probably. The numbers are certainly going up with time. But perhaps the better way of putting that is we're "confirming" more tornadoes that otherwise might have been missed many years ago. As our climate continues to change, what's considered "normal" will continue to evolve. This, alongside continued improvements in technology, will make it very difficult for apples to apples comparisons to the past.

No Signs of Fall…

This Summer doesn’t have an off button. I know it was disappointing that Southeast Texas received 27” of rain and North Texas got little to nothing. Yesterday’s “cooler day” still managed a high of 94 with 102 heat index. Average highs are 92 right now now and drop into the 80s starting next Sunday. 

Mother Nature has other plans this year and Texas doesn’t do “normal” weather very well. The dreaded ridge is coming back and it’s massive for September. Rain free and triple digits return. Not record territory for Labor Day weekend, but records start coming down late next week to 101 range and that’s doable to break. Lows near 80
and highs in the low 100s are the dog days of Summer weather. The extended dry streak continues for the foreseeable future. 

The light at the end of the tunnel would be to get one of these Pacific storms to turn North and get caught up in the jet stream to slingshot into Texas. We need something big to disrupt this weather pattern and I’m not seeing it until Fall actually gets here.

MAJOR CATEGORY 4 HURRICANE LOWELL⚠️Major Hurricane Lowell bears watching closely through the Labor Day weekend if you're a resident of or visiting Hawaii! Lowell remains a Category 4 Hurricane with sustained winds of 130 mph, and gusts of 160 mph, located about 495 miles south-southwest of Hilo tonight. The Hurricane is moving west but is forecast to slow before making a sharp turn toward the northwest and north this weekend.

That turn will be critical. Lowell could move near the western Hawaiian Islands late Sunday through Monday night, potentially still as a Major Hurricane, but confidence remains low on exactly how close the center will come to the Islands, and impacts could range from minor to major depending on where and when that northward turn occurs. A positive note is that there has been a slight westward jog in guidance which would keep Lowell a little farther away from Hawaii.

Even without a direct hit, however, of Hawaii could experience dangerous surf, coastal flooding-storm surge, strong winds and heavy rainfall, with the greatest concern currently toward the western end of the State, particularly Kauai County. Coastal inundation could also be worsened by peak monthly high tides Monday. Swells from Lowell will produce increasingly dangerous, potentially life-threatening surf and rip currents over the next several days.

There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect at this time but everyone in Hawaii should closely monitor Lowell through the weekend and have Hurricane plans and supplies ready. The forecast should become clearer as the Hurricane approaches its expected turn north⚠️

MONITORING MARIE🌧️🌴Hurricane Marie is expected to remain well offshore of California, but its tropical moisture could influence parts of the state and other parts of the West in multiple waves over the next week.

The first push arrives this weekend, with tropical moisture increasing across Southern California late Saturday into Sunday. Sunday currently looks like the wetter day, with showers and a few thunderstorms possible, including for coastal areas and valleys and mountains-coastal slopes. Moisture will spread inland as well, increasing shower and thunderstorm chances across the deserts and parts of Nevada, and other parts of the West.

Then attention turns to mid-to-late next week. Over the past day, there has been a noticeable trend in some guidance toward eventually turning Marie or its weakening circulation northward over the eastern Pacific. This is not currently the official forecast and remains highly uncertain, but it is worth watching. Marie would be weakening and remain well offshore, but a northward turn could help pull its remnant tropical moisture into California mid week and beyond. Higher confidence in the evolution of Marie will develop over the coming days🌧️🌴

items.text: HIT-OR-MISS STORMS POSSIBLE ACROSS THE NORTHWEST FRIDAY⛈️a cool upper-level storm will remain over the Northwest Friday, keeping the atmosphere unstable enough for scattered showers and thunderstorms. items.text:
RAIN & ISO. FLOOD RISK SATURDAY NIGHT-MONDAY🌧️⚠️a large Pacific storm will interact with tropical moisture from Hurricane Marie this weekend, bringing an increase in rain and thunderstorms from Southern California and the Southwest into the Great Basin and Northern U.S. Rockies. Sunday looks like the main flash-flood day across the Southwest and Great Basin. Moisture will increase across Southern California, especially the mountains and deserts, before becoming deeper across southeast California, northwest Arizona, Nevada and Utah. Utah could be one of the main areas to watch, with widespread thunderstorms and locally heavy rainfall capable of flash flooding, particularly across central and southern portions of the state.

By Sunday night into Monday, the Pacific low will start to move inland and pull moisture farther north and east into eastern Utah, western Colorado, Wyoming, Idaho and the Northern U.S. Rockies. Heavy rainfall and localized flash flooding will remain possible, especially over higher terrain and areas with saturated soils or burn scars. Idaho should see more widespread precipitation late Sunday into Monday, although current guidance favors the deepest tropical moisture passing farther south and east through Utah and Wyoming. Much cooler air will also arrive Monday, potentially bringing a rain/snow mix to the highest peaks Monday across the Inland Northwest into the Northern U.S. Rockies.

Not everyone will see flooding, and not everyone will see rain, but burn scars, slot canyons, normally dry washes and steep terrain will be particularly vulnerable to rapid runoff. The exact corridor of heaviest rain will continue to become clearer over the next couple of days🌧️⚠️

HAWAII WIND RISK INCREASING FROM LOWELL🌺🌀the greatest concern is increasingly focused on Kauai and the western end of the island chain late Monday into Monday night. While the exact track of Lowell’s northward turn remains uncertain, current guidance suggests it could move close enough to bring at least tropical-storm-force winds to portions of Hawaii. Even a relatively small shift east or west in Lowell’s eventual track could substantially change these probabilities. The latest 5-day wind-probability forecast, the chance of sustained tropical-storm-force winds from Major Hurricane Lowell has increased for parts of Hawaii, especially the western islands. The latest probabilities are around 50-60% near Barking Sands on Kauai, 30-40% near Lihue, and 10-20% near Honolulu. The probabilities rise sharply west of the islands, reflecting Lowell’s expected turn northward early next week.

It’s important to note that Hawaii is already experiencing strong, gusty trade winds, partly due to the pressure gradient between Lowell to the south and strong high pressure to the north. Those current winds are different from the potential direct tropical-storm-force winds from Lowell shown in this probability graphic🌺🌀

3 HURRICANES ACROSS THE EASTERN & CENTRAL PACIFIC🌀🌀🌀 the Pacific is extremely active this morning with Hurricanes Marie, Karina and Lowell all spinning at the same time, and while none are currently forecast to make a direct hit [Hawaii does need to monitor Lowell closely]  on the U.S. mainland, each could influence weather from Hawaii to California and the Southwest over the coming days.

🌺 HAWAII - LOWELL IS THE BIG ONE TO WATCH: Major Hurricane Lowell is passing several hundred miles south of Hawaii, but the forecast becomes much more concerning early next week. Lowell is expected to slow and then make a sharp turn north, potentially while still a major hurricane. Lowell could move near the westernmost main Hawaiian Islands late Monday into Monday night, with the potential for wind, heavy rain, storm surge and very large surf depending on exactly where that turn occurs. Residents across Hawaii should closely monitor the forecast through the weekend and make sure hurricane plans and supplies are ready.

Hurricane Karina is farther east and is expected to eventually pass north/northeast of Hawaii. A direct impact currently appears less likely, but Karina will send a large swell toward the islands, potentially producing high-end advisory or warning-level surf along east-facing shores this weekend. With both Karina and Lowell interacting with the larger-scale pattern around Hawaii, forecast uncertainty remains elevated.

🌴CALIFORNIA & THE SOUTHWEST - WATCH MARIE: Hurricane Marie is moving west-northwest well southwest of Baja California. A direct strike on Southern California is not expected, but Marie's moisture and swells could still have noticeable impacts. Large surf is expected to reach Southern California this weekend, while tropical moisture streaming northward could increase clouds, showers and thunderstorms across portions of Southern California.

That moisture will also be drawn into the Southwest, combining with the broader monsoon pattern. Rain and thunderstorm chances increase across Arizona and eventually southeast California this weekend. The Weather Prediction Center has outlined an excessive rain risk across a good part of the Southwest as atmospheric moisture climbs well above normal, meaning locally heavy thunderstorms and isolated flash flooding will be possible🌀🌴🌧️

Tropical Storm Edouard delivered a powerful punch to parts of Texas over the last couple of days. 20-30" of rain accumulated in a very short period of time in a small area of East Texas.

In Hardin County, 21 people had to be evacuated from an assisted living facility after flood waters threatened the building the people were in. 

The storm also brought strong winds that downed trees & powerlines in some locations, where 70-90 mph wind gusts were reported. 

Edouard is no longer an organized system, but its moisture & rain remain in the region & will help enhance rainfall rates with pop-up storms. 

Images: Texas Game Wardens
